x174nbbf.author: Plutarch
x174nbbf.label: The five names of Apollo
x174nbbf.translation: Since therefore this God is no less a philosopher than a prophet, Ammonius seemed to all of us rightly to apply every one of his names to this purpose, and to teach that he is Pythius (or a questionist ) to those who begin to learn and enquire; Delius and Phanaeus (or a manifester and prover ) to those to whom somewhat of the truth is already manifest and shines forth; Ismenius (or knowing ) to those that have acquired knowledge; and Leschenorius (or discoursing ) when they practise and enjoy their science, making use of it to discourse and philosophize with one another.
x174nbbf.translator: R. Kippax, in W. W. Goodwin (ed.), Plutarch's Morals, vol. IV (1874)
x174nbbf.reading: She treats the names as five steps of the awakening of consciousness, Pythios, Delios, Phanaios, Ismenios, Leschenorios (she separates Delios and Phanaios), joined by the four etymologies of Apollo in the Cratylus: four plus five makes nine, the ennead, "the new one". The god appears differently according to where the seeker stands.

x8j6sc6.translation: I do not believe that any single name could have been better adapted to express the attributes of the God, embracing and in a manner signifying all four of them,--music, and prophecy, and medicine, and archery. ... has reference to all the powers of the God, who is the single one, the everdarting, the purifier, the mover together (aplous, aei Ballon, apolouon, omopolon).

x10u8sna.author: Plutarch
x10u8sna.label: Know thyself, and the answer: Thou art
x10u8sna.translation: For the God in a manner calls upon every one of us who comes hither, with this salutation, Know thyself, which is nothing inferior to All hail. And we again, answering the God, say to him Εἶ , thou art; attributing to him the true, unfeigned, and sole appellation of being, as agreeing to him alone.
x10u8sna.translator: R. Kippax, in W. W. Goodwin (ed.), Plutarch's Morals, vol. IV (1874)
x10u8sna.reading: Pilgrims came to know the god, and instead of a welcome Apollo says: if you want to know me, know yourself. Beside it stands ΕΙ, "you are": you already are the divinity you seek inside the temple. She also notes that the precept says "thyself" in the singular, pointing to one Self, consciousness turning its eye on itself.

beats.beat: Apollo's temple bears 'Know thyself'.

beats.beat: The command is in the singular and may be read 'know it'.

x1nkuohs.author: Plutarch
x1nkuohs.label: Apollo: denying the many
x1nkuohs.translation: For the Divinity is not many, as every one of us is made of ten thousand differences in affections, being a confused heap, filled with all diversities. But that which is must be one, as one must have a being. But diversity, which is esteemed to be different from being, goes forth to the generation of that which is not. Whence both the first of his names agrees rightly with this God, as do also the second and third. For he is called Apollo, as denying plurality and rejecting multitude; and Ieïos, as being only one;
x1nkuohs.translator: R. Kippax, in W. W. Goodwin (ed.), Plutarch's Morals, vol. IV (1874)
x1nkuohs.reading: She reads Ἀπόλλων as ἀ- plus πολλῶν, "not of the many", and says the Pythagoreans used Apollo as the code name for the One, as Plutarch and Plotinus report. Apollo invites us out of dualist views into a field where subject, object, self and other coexist in one illumination.
